title: maniMon: a workstation monitor with persistent statistics and honest per-run cost accounting
description:
maniMon is a Linux workstation monitor for machines that run long jobs. Two docked GTK panels, a headless recorder, and a small privileged sensor sampler.

It exists because the usual answer to "how hot did the GPU get during last night's run, and what did it cost in watt-hours" is that nobody kept the data: sparklines in a system monitor are ring buffers inside a process, and restarting the process erases the history.

Sensors most monitors do not read. The amdgpu gpu_metrics binary v1_3 sysfs structure, giving the three voltage-regulator temperatures, the throttle status word, and average versus current clocks — none of which appear in hwmon. Struct offsets were determined empirically from live bytes on an RDNA 3 card and cross-checked field by field against independent hwmon readings, rather than taken from a header. Also the BMC via IPMI (chassis fans, board and per-DIMM temperatures and power, rails), SMART for NVMe and SATA, ECC counters, PSI pressure, RAPL package power, and the DIMM inventory from DMI — the last of these showing which memory channels are populated, and therefore how much of the controller's bandwidth is actually reachable.

Persistent statistics. A SQLite store with three resolutions folded by age (10 s for 48 h, 1 min for 30 days, 10 min indefinitely), roughly 400 MB per year with retention enforced on every fold. Rates are averaged when downsampled; temperatures and power take the maximum, because averaging a thermal peak away defeats the purpose of keeping history. This yields dated peaks, p95, energy in watt-hours by trapezoid integration with gap detection, and the fraction of time spent above a named threshold.

Per-run accounting, and what it refuses to claim. Exclusive quantities — CPU-seconds, peak resident memory, peak thread count, wall time — are measured from each process's own counters and are genuinely attributable to a run even when runs overlap. Shared quantities — GPU power and energy, junction temperature, package watts — are machine-wide and are deliberately never divided between concurrent runs: one GPU feeding three jobs draws one board power, and splitting it three ways would invent a number no sensor measured. Shared figures are instead reported alongside the peak concurrency observed during the run's window.

Honesty about units. SMART attribute 241 is vendor-defined: drives count 512-byte LBAs, 32 MiB chunks, or whole gibibytes under the same identifier, and some report a unit-free count while still naming the attribute Total_LBAs_Written. Read one such drive as LBAs and it claims three megabytes written across 3420 power-on hours. maniMon therefore publishes the raw counter together with the attribute name and derives a byte figure only where the unit is established, marking inferred values as approximate. Attribute 194 receives the same treatment: its raw field packs current, minimum and maximum temperature into one integer, which is how monitors come to report a disk at 210 billion degrees.

Privilege. The panels never run as root. A single auditable script runs as root on a timer and writes world-readable JSON into a tmpfs directory; the panels read files and never gain privilege.

Colour palettes for light and dark themes are measured rather than eyeballed: contrast ratios are checked against WCAG by a runnable self-test, and categorical colours are validated under simulated protanopia, deuteranopia and tritanopia.
